utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kay, is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour, and I call Mr. Borislav Skegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Perhaps we could use our time in between. Mr. Mikulicic, we have looked at The Blue Book, some parts on the ELMO. Now, it seems that in the electronic version of The Blue Book, we do not see certain portions which are there in the hard copy. Would it be possible to have a look at the hard copy, just to start with, for comparison reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I believe that's possible, Your Honour. But as we said, we are not intent to enter The Blue Booked into the evidence. That was a Prosecution intent. So I believe if there is something to be clarified The Blue Book, it is up to the party that would like to introduce The Blue Book into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first, for one second, I was just filling the time available. I will come back to this at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skegro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Skegro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will be first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, you speak the English language, but as I understand it, you would prefer to give your testimony in your own tongue.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. The matters are serious and one wishes to be as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just say that so that the Court is clear. Mr. Skegro, you gave a statement to the Defence, is that correct, for these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we call up 2D00721, which will go on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I believe you have a hard copy in front of you, Mr. Skegro; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you see a witness statement on the screen on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we can go down to the bottom of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that your signature beneath it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you confirm that this is the statement that you gave to the Defence and signed. And perhaps we could look at the end of the statement to the last page, where there is a date and a final signature.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, this is that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless requires it of me, each and every page is signed in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, were there three minor corrections that you needed to make to that statement, one of which you told me about today, but the other two, when I met you on the 8th of September to confirm the contents of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes. We are indeed talking about three minor corrections, but let's be precise and let's correct them nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The parties have all been given a notice about this, and I will lead you through it. So if we just go to paragraph 3, line 28 to 31, of the English translation, and it's lines 21 to 24 in the Croatian original, was there a correction that you wanted to make to the text there so that it read: "The office of the president was responsible for four ministries, the Ministry of Defence, of the interior, foreign affairs, and of finance. The ministers for three, Mr. Susak, Mr. Granic, and Mr. Jarnjak, reported to the prime minister, Mr. Valentic, and to President Tudjman." Is that a correction that you wanted to make to your original statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes. There were four state ministries. The Ministry of Defence, of the interior, foreign affairs, and of finance. And here it -- you can see that only three ministries are indicated and the ministry of finance is missing. However, in practice, the president, together with the prime minister, directly coordinated the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and of Defence, and the Ministry of Finance in a certain way, in that distribution of work was within the purview of the government headed by Minister Valentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skegro, we're in a court, where what we say is translated and that requires us to speak at times at a much slower pace than we are used to, and I saw you looking at me when I was stopping in my sentences but that was because I was allowing others to translate in sections.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I apologise, I'll try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we turn to paragraph 11, line 24, in the English translation; line 29 in the Croatian original, should it read: "We returned from Drnis to Split and then by aeroplane to Zagreb."

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a further matter you told me about this morning, in the English, paragraph 4, line 33. Instead of the word "army," it should be "Ministry of Defence"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: That's correct. "The Ministry of Defence," full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, taking into account those corrections to your original statement, if I was to ask you the questions again today that enabled you to give the answers that are contained within your statement, would your answers today be the same as when you originally made your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: They would be completely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Your Honour, I move that the witness statement be put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, this suggests -- and I don't think you asked the witness that he gave his statement to the best of his recollection and in accordance with the truth, because the last question and answer do not mean very much if that has not been established. May I take it that you gave your statement at the time to the best of your recollection and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also that what is put on paper reflects what you said at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think -- Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. I do not hear of any objections from the other Defence teams. Mr. Registrar, the statement of Mr. Skegro.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1679.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1679 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, I have no further questions to ask you today, but others may, so please remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to read the summary now or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do it now with the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. The statement of Borislav Skegro, in a summary form, is -- is as follows. That on the 3rd of April, 1993, he was appointed deputy prime minister of the Republic of Croatia for the economy. Also, on the 11th of September, 1997, he became the finance minister, and he remained in both of those positions until the year 2000. When he was appointed deputy prime minister, Mr. Cermak was the minister of industry, shipbuilding, and energy. As Mr. Skegro was the deputy prime minister for the economy, he oversaw the economic sector of the government and was responsible for the ministries of finance, industry, shipbuilding, energy, agriculture, tourism, and construction. So whilst he was the deputy prime minister for the economy, Mr. Cermak, whilst a minister, was subordinated to him. Mr. Cermak had told him that he would be a minister for only a few months and that he would later be replaced by someone else, and that in October 1993, Mr. Cermak left the government and Mr. Skegro had no further dealings with him directly but he knew that he was in the oil business with his own private company. On 4th August 1995, when Operation Storm started, he was on vacation but he had had strong indications that something would happen, although he was not involved in the planning. On that day, he talked to the prime minister, Mr. Valentic, around noon, and he was asked to return urgently to Zagreb. He arrived in Zagreb around midnight on the 4th of August. On the 5th of August, at around 10.00, he was with the prime minister in his office when he learnt that Knin had been liberated. President Tudjman called Prime Minister Valentic and they congratulated each other on the telephone. Around noon, he went to Tuskanac with President Tudjman and other ministers, where they met. There was Mr. Granic, Mr. Susak, Mr. Jarnjak, Mr. Radic, Mr. Pasalic, and others. They were all the members of the government who were in Zagreb at that time, and they followed the news reports about the Croatian Army entering Knin several hours before. During that time, Mr. Galbraith called and talked to Minister Susak and gave congratulations for the Operation Storm. President Tudjman said at one stage, We must find a person and send him to Knin, somebody who will integrate and resuscitate the economy, with the experience of a former minister, establish communication with the UN and the international community, somebody who will have knowledge in military logistics who speaks a foreign language, a multi-dimensional person. Some people recommend Ivan Cermak to me. Ivan has experience in private business, was an assistant minister of defence. He has an untypical style for a general, and he will establish relations with the UN and the international community. That is how Mr. Cermak was appointed the commander of the Knin garrison. His job was to establish communication with the UN and bring life back to normal, provide the services for the town. Therefore, civilian logistics within the army. "I agreed that this was a very good choice. I believe that President Tudjman wanted to send a message to them that we wanted the Serbs to stay and that we encourage reconstruction." Mr. Skegro states that normalisation included the return of persons displaced in 1991 as well as those who left their homes in 1995. It was meant for all, and the mandate was to help all people, regardless of ethnic affiliation. The normalisation in Knin was important for normalisation in the rest of Croatia because of the strategic positioning of the town Knin within the state of Croatia. At that time, in 1995, money was needed to normalise life. He was attempting to get a loan on the international money markets to prevent the collapse of the national currency. It was necessary to activate companies as soon as possible; for example, the Tvik factory, and other factories which used to operate in Knin. The purpose of sending Mr. Cermak to Knin was to get the whole system to start functioning as soon as possible for the benefit of the town and the whole Croatian economy. Mr. Skegro visited Knin with President Tudjman on the 6th of August. There was a lunch on that day, and after lunch he walked around the town and visited several locations, and then he went to visit Drnis. The next time he visited Knin was on the 26th of August on the freedom train, from Zagreb, via Knin, to Split, when President Tudjman, members of the government, politicians, actors, public figures, academics, businessmen, and others, were also on the train. On the 7th of September, 1995, he visited Knin again to attend a session of the Croatian government which was held in the town. About five or six such sessions had been held outside the capital, Zagreb, and all members of the government were present at the session in Knin where the agenda concerned establishment, functioning of civilian authorities in liberated areas, reconstruction, information about the return and other matters. On his way back to Zagreb, he travelled by bus, and he saw some houses on fire, and smoke, near Korenica. He saw some ten dead sheep by the road. He and Prime Minister Valentic commented about what kind of person could have done that and what could be done to prevent that from happening in the future. They wondered who was starting the fires and looting. He states that there was a period when Croatia had been occupied for four years and the government had not had control of its territory during that period, and no government could be perfectly organised in such conditions. It was the job of the government to establish law and order in the area. The minister of the interior sent additional forces to make sure that perpetrators of crimes were arrested and prosecuted, and a formal decision had been taken by the government by which Minister Jarnjak explicitly took over responsibility for the whole territory as of the 6th of August, 1995. He states that Mr. Cermak could not have been part of a joint criminal enterprise, because there was no such joint criminal enterprise. The government, in which he was the deputy prime minister, was not involved in any such plan. If there had been such a plan, he believed he would have been informed, considering his position at the time. He is sure that a motive of personal revenge was responsible for what took place. Your Honour, that concludes my summary of Mr. Skegro's statement and as the Court knows, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kehoe, do you want to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, yes. You would like to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Kay has read out the summary which reflects what was told in everything but two minor details. It may seem like hair-splitting but let me explain. When there's a list of people who were present at the Tuskanac on 5th of August, together with President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, what is in evidence is your statement, to the extent there may be minor imprecisions in what Mr. Kay said, that it's mainly to inform the public, and Mr. Kay is rather detailed in his summaries, unlike some other parties. So, therefore, as far as evidence is concerned, you don't have to bother. If there's anything triggered by the reading of the summary by Mr. Kay that you say, No, my statement must have been misunderstood or is incorrect, then we'd like to hear from you. But hair-splitting exercises just for what is to inform the public about what is basically to be found in your statement, it being only your statement that is in evidence and not the summary. So if you want to correct anything, please proceed, but, if it is just the way in which the summary was phrased, then unless it creates real confusion, then I would suggest that we would proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just a minor point and I will -- I withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're ready to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Skegro, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe, and Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skegro. Mr. Skegro, I would like to just ask you a few questions and draw on your experience and your expertise as the deputy prime minister of economy, and I would like to focus, if we can, on paragraph 8 of your statement, where you are discussing the economic impact of control of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to that. Should be page 6 in the English and I'm not quite sure what it is in the B/C/S. That's the page in the English, thank you, yeah. Ta.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skegro, if I may, towards the bottom of the paragraph 8, where you're talking about -- I assume talking about the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina and Knin, you note that: "It was possible to control all flows of goods and trade in Knin, as well as passenger travel from one part of the country to another. We were blockaded, and if we tried to calculate the economic loss sustained by the Republic of Croatia, the physical destruction of production capacity in the Republic of Croatia and that bypass road which you had to take every time you travelled to Dalmatia, the loss would be enormous." Now, Mr. Skegro, the Chamber has received some evidence on the economic impact that the continued existence of the so-called Republic of Serb Krajina had on the Republic of Croatia and how that was negatively impacting the economic growth of the country. Can you elaborate on that just a bit and -- and dovetail it with this particular paragraph on what was happening in your experience as the deputy minister of economics while the so-called Republic of Serb Krajina continued in its incident existence? And what was happening, I'm talking about economically?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Anybody who looks at the geographical map of Croatia, where they're railroads and main roads drawn in, will realise that once the Knin area was blocked off, and that lasted from August 1990 onwards, and basically cut off -- cut Croatia into two separate parts, so that when the war broke out in 1991, and when the bridge connecting the island of Pag with the land was seriously damaged, the entire Dalmatia, to the south of the island of Pag, in the economical sense and in practical sense could be considered an island which one could reach only by a ferry from Zigljen and then by driving 60 or 70 kilometres on Pag and then by crossing via one, I repeat, one lane of the Pag bridge which hadn't been destroyed and then travelling onwards. This is to say that when Knin was not integrated in the Republic of Croatia was simply a blocked off area that had -- that stood no chance of having any economic success. It also inflicted significant economic damage on Croatia, and I don't want to bandy about any figures, in terms of millions of dollars, kunas and so on, but if one were to calculate it, and even if one were to forget the entire damage caused by war, then one would reach really significant amounts, billions and billions of euros, without mentioning how it affected tourism. There was basically no tourism in Dalmatia during that period of time because nobody wanted to travel to a country that was either a state of war or in -- in imminent state -- threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, just if I may, just comment on your last answer where you talked about the entire damage caused by the war and then one -- if one would forget the entire damage caused by war and then one would reach really significant amounts, billions and billions of euros, without how it affected tourism. Is it your assessment -- without coming to exact figures, Mr. Skegro, and heaven knows, I'm not asking you that, but is your assessment, as you look back at that time, as -- in your role as the -- the deputy prime minister for economy, was your assessment that there was in fact billions and billions of euros in damage to the Republic of Croatia during this time-frame when the Republic -- the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina was in existence?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Naturally, if somebody wanted a comprehensive and more precise information about the damage, then the republican Croatia, sometime in 1997 or 1998, adopted an official document which was a report of the Commission on War Damage. A separate government commission had been established, and after the war this commission listed down all cases of direct damage, destruction during wartime as well as indirect damage caused by the lack of economic activity and then expenses related to refugees, and so on, and all of these figures can be found in one document. And if I remember well, the entire figure mentioned at the time was 270 billion kunas, up until either 1996 or 1997. Therefore, in order to give you a perspective on what 270 billion kunas is, that would be approximately two annual gross domestic product of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President, if that came through clearly on the translation to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you repeat that last comment, Mr. Skegro, about the 270 billion kuna?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had no difficulties. I understood that it was -- the national product for two years, which is a gross national product which is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I got that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- standardly used expression in economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So what we're talking about is two years of GNP, gross national product. One last question on this score. In your para -- the paragraph in the translation, where you talked about -- in paragraph 8, where you talk about Knin being a cross-roads town, about midway through that paragraph you note that: "The town of Knin itself, if it is cut off and not part of Croatia is insignificant. If it is in the Republic of Croatia, it is connected to Zagreb, and it connects to [sic] Zadar, Sibenik, Bosnia and Herzegovina?" In the context of this, what are you talking about the town of Knin itself being insignificant?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Well, the town did not come about outside of Croatia and it would serve no purpose if were not located there, at the cross-roads of valleys and so on. If -- you may know that, during medieval times, Knin was founded in an area where there are natural cross-roads of valleys and rivers and so on. It's the natural environment surrounding it, and this is why the town was founded, and if you cut it off, then this natural reason for its existence will be gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. One additional question, the kuna at the time was -- compared to the dollar or to the Deutschemark was approximately how much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe it or not, exactly the same exchange rate as today, approximately 1 German mark was 3.7 kunas at the time. If we multiply that by 1.955883, which is the exchange rate between euro and German mark, then you would see approximately the -- today's exchange rate between kuna and euro which is one -- that one -- that 1 euro is 7.3 kunas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which then means that we are talking about approximately 40 million -- 40 billion euros. That is 40.000 million euros. That's just for my --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- own understanding. That's approximately the number we are talking about, which means 20.000 million or 20 billion euros is the gross -- the yearly gross national product of Croatia. Is that correctly concluded? You said two gross national products a year? I'm just trying to verify whether my understanding of the number is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, you understood this perfectly. I understood you in English, and despite some minor imprecisions in interpretation you were correct. 40 billion euros approximately equals 270 billion kunas, and that was equal to two annual GDPs in the 1990s of the last century, in 1995 and 1996. To give you another comparison, this is approximately this year's annual GDP of Croatia because, fortunately, in the meantime, Croatia has made significant progress and its annual GDP has doubled in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any questions for Mr. Skegro?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will be short, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, you will be now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skegro.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just a few things I needed to clarify with you, and I would kindly ask you to make sure you have a small break between question and answer so as to enable the interpreters to do their job properly. Mr. Skegro, I will now refer to paragraph 14 of your statement given to the Defence of General Cermak. And in that paragraph you speak of how the Croatian government did not have control of the area of the so-called republic of Krajina for four years. The area was later liberated in Operation Storm, and you say that you personally - and you say this in line 26, paragraph 14, of the Croatian version - so you say that with police forces that Croatia had at its disposal, "we could not successfully cover such a large territory which suddenly became free." Could you please elaborate on that? What did you mean by this? What did you mean by this statement, by this phrase in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Very simply, before Operation Storm we had a territory of 100 territorial units, let's say, and you covered it with 100 policemen. Several days after that, you have 130 territorial units and still just 100 policemen. That's what I meant by this. Simply speaking, the then existing police forces by definition were not sufficient to cover this additional territory, or, rather, to cover it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, you, as member of the government, did you ever witness or did you ever feel that the Croatian authorities, and I'm now referring mostly to the government and Ministry of Interior, were not putting in sufficient effort to control that area by means of police force, that there was some tacit or -- agreement to tolerate these crimes which took place after the completion of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, there are two questions in this question of yours and I will try to deal with them one by one. The first question, as I can see from the English transcript, is, whether, based on my best recollection, Croatian government put in sufficient effort to enable the police to control this newly liberated area, and my answer to that question is yes. Your second question is whether, in my opinion, there was some kind of a tacit agreement to tolerate the crimes that may have happened, and my explicit answer to that is no. And now that you have asked me this, I feel the need to say here, in this venue, that, had I ever felt that somewhere in Croatia, in the government, in some circles, there was such a way of thinking or let alone such an agreement, I would not have spent a single minute with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Skegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Russo, Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Hedaraly apparently. Mr. Skegro, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can I have 65 ter 2807 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, what you will see on the screen appearing is a transcript of a meeting at the presidential palace on 11 April 1995. And will you see on the first page that you were one of the persons present at that meeting. If we now go to page 71 in the English, page 70 in the B/C/S, there's a statement that you make that I want to read to you and then ask you a question about it. You say: "And then a question arises, Mr. President, shall I go to Washington and lie to those people? If it is for the benefit of Croatia, I will lie to the Pope, just as I had lied flatly in the parliament when asked why the budget had taken a loan with the national bank, because we knew what it was. It was for the weapons. I said, as cool as a cucumber, that it was for the stabilisation programme and I don't know what else." Now, Mr. Skegro, in the transcript of that recording, you admitted having lied to the Croatian parliament and that you would be willing to lie to anyone, including the Pope. Can you tell this Chamber why they should not think that you're lying today?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I would kindly ask you to split this text of what I purportedly said. Frankly speaking, I think that I did say this, I did utter these words, although in the transcripts one never know what was left out and what was added. But as I'm reading this now, I can tell you that, yes, I could have phrased this in these terms as read out here. We have to look at the context, Mr. Prosecutor, and I have the Croatian version before me now in which I say that I'm not going to go and lie to these people in Washington. That's my first sentence. I'm saying, Mr. President, I'm not going to Washington to go and lie to these people. That is my request to the president. And if you let me look at the transcript, two pages back, perhaps I could refresh my memory as to the context. But I think that I do remember, based on the date, what was the main topic of this meeting. And then my second sentence that you put to me, where I say, If necessary, for the welfare of Croatia, I will lie even to the Pope. You will allow me that this is rhetorics. This is a figure of speech. I don't need to explain this any further. And then I go on to say, Just as I lied in Sabor in the parliament, and what the budget was for, with the national bank because we knew what it was, it was weapons. Mr. Prosecutor, as you know, Croatia had to arm itself in secret because there was a resolution of the Security Council of the UN - I'm not going to comment upon it, I'm not going to comment on why and how - but this resolution forbade Croatia, which was unarmed, to arm itself. So any weaponry that arrived Croatia was in violation of this resolution of the Security Council. You don't really expect me to state in front of the Croatian parliament that, at that time, we were violating the resolution of the UN Security Council. Yes, we did. Those were the times, those were the circumstances, and if I were to find myself in the same circumstances again, I would have done the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, you're not denying making that statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 2807 into evidence, and, Mr. President, we have a truncated version as well which only covers the first page and this page. I don't know if the parties want to add more pages for context. The quote is really the only thing that we are concerned. That would be 65 ter 2807A, but I leave that in the hands of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two issues, Mr. Hedaraly. The first one is that the witness apparently challenges the translation, or at least interprets his own words in a different way from what it looks, Shall I go to Washington and lie to those people, whether that is an expression of willingness to do so or, rather, reluctance to do so; that's the first issue. The second issue is that if we only have the quote, then we do not know what the witness is either reluctant or willing to lie for. So, therefore, we would need a bit more of context to better understand the context of all this. So, therefore, I'm -- I would like to consider with my colleagues whether we can do just with the quote. I think cover page is fine, but I will look for some more context. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Plainly the translation needs to be looked at, so if this document is marked for identification, let the parties look at the translation, look at the whole transcript for further context, that may assist the Court on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that there will be no need, in view of the fact that the Prosecution is focussing that much on the quote, that the full 120 pages should be -- they are translated already, Mr. Hedaraly? Yes. So there's no -- nevertheless, to have to read through 120 pages if only a couple are relevant might not be a good idea. So the parties are invited to -- apart from checking the translation, also to further consider what would give the appropriate context for the Chamber to understand the testimony of the witness. Mr. Registrar, could you assign a MFI number to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit P2640, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Skegro, at paragraph 7, you state that you were one of the witnesses of the way in which Mr. Cermak was appointed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that was on the 5th of August, at a meeting in Tuskanac?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that you were involved in that decision?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say how much my opinion influenced -- influenced Mr. President's decision. But I agreed with all his arguments when he spoke about the characteristics of a person who would be sent to Knin. I agreed that Ivan Cermak was a suitable person for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you know, Mr. Skegro, that the president had actually made the decision to send General Cermak to Knin on the previous day, on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: No. However, if anyone among us opposed to the decision at the meeting, knowing President Tudjman, I believe that he might have even changed that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Cermak was formally appointed as garrison commander of the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 7418, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: This is another presidential transcript meeting, this time dated 2 July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to page 36 in the B/C/S; page 29 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I will let you read where you start your intervention. And then when we go to the next page, there's a portion I want to -- actually why don't you read it, tell us when you -- we can go to the next page. I think your full statement lasts a page and a half or two pages. Read it, and then I want to focus on specific portions so you have the full benefit of what you said.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Can you turn the page, please. Turn the page, please. I have read the Croatian version of the text, and drawing my lessons from our previous discussion, I would like to see the English version, because, Your Honours, the English translation in the previous text was exactly contrary to what I said. In Croatian the words are "I'm not going lie," and in the English version it says, "I am going to lie." I had given up on some minor imprecisions but this is a crucial thing. If you want me to do so I can comment upon the Croatian version of what I have just read and then can you ask me questions, and then depending on what your questions are going to be, I will probably go back and ask for the English version to see what your questions may be based on. If I decide there are ambiguities in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: This is what I propose to do: I will read a portion of that in English, so you will have that benefit, and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the parties are invited to the highly contested line from before the break, whether he would go and lie or whether he would not go and lie, that to be checked already during the first break perhaps with the assistance -- it's focussing really on one line, to seek the assistance of CLSS and see whether there is any -- any way to resolve that -- that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go back -- two pages back in the English, please, and one page back in the B/C/S, and at the -- one more page back, please, in the English. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now at the bottom of that page, the last paragraph starts -- and that's the portion I want to read from you: "Aside from Mr. President read out about these terrible realities of the English policy and beyond, I would only remind you by drawing a parallel with what Willy Brandt said on the Berlin Wall the night when it was practically torn to down. He said, Those who belong together are to live together. I only say it goes the other way around too. Those who do not belong together will not live together. From everything I know in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or in Yugoslavia, no matter what we think, whether it is civilised, whether it's like this or like that, and not only because of the atrocities that have taken place, there is no core existence. There is no Bosnia-Herzegovina." And my question for you, Mr. Skegro, is: What you've expressed about people not belonging together, not living together, did you feel the same way about the Serbs in Croatia, that they did not belong there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. Since you have decided to use this quote, I'd like to say that, to the best of my recollection, that quote is correct. This is more or less what I indeed did say. Unfortunately, as we all know today, I was right. Look at Bosnia and Herzegovina today and you will see how it manages to exist. The point of my discussion was this. With all -- all the historical encumbrances, the differences, Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state without an international umbrella or protectorate could not exist. And as you can see for yourself today, unfortunately, and I repeat, unfortunately I was absolutely right, and I was talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina, mind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, if you would not mind, would you please answer the question that was put to you. You were not asked to comment on how realistic your views were in view of the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But the question was whether you did feel the same way about the Serbs in Croatia; that is, that people, not belonging together, that they would or should not live together. That was the question that was put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not what I meant either at the time or now. At that -- I never implied Serbs in Croatia. We shouldn't confuse things and compare in an appropriate way situations in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. As you know, in Bosnia and Herzegovina there existed and still exists three constituent people, Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks, which was not the case in Croatia, never has been. So to draw such parallels may be useful where if you want it discredit your witness but it really does not have any bearing on the reality, and it does not stem from the reality at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can I tender 65 ter 7418 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be appropriate, again, if it is marked for identification so that we could see if there 's any further parts of the transcript that ought to be put in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be no translation issue but for contextualisation and for carefully selecting the relevant portions, Mr. Hedaraly, may I take it that you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2641, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You had discussed in your statement your view that there was no joint criminal enterprise, and I just want to ask you a few questions. You were on the Brioni island on 31 July 1995, were you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't on the Brioni island on that day. I did not belong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you were not at the meeting that President Tudjman had with his military advisors on that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Correct. I was not at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you were also not involved -- would it be also correct to say that you were not involved in the planning of the Storm military operation at all?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Nowhere in the world is this part of the job of the deputy prime minister in charge of economy and finances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of everywhere in the world but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, it seems that, for one reason or another, you feel a need to criticise the one who questions you, at least implicitly. I think Mr. Hedaraly was just seeking confirmation whether you were involved or not and what happens in the rest of the world, I think the simple answer would have been, No, I was not involved in it. Isn't it? Then we keep matters as --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in paragraph 14 of your statement, and Mr. Mikulicic referred to a sentence there about the availability of the police forces. In the English, it was at line 28 to 30. And the following line you write or you stated: "Operation Storm took place several months after Operation Flash and we had no experience." I'm just seeking clarification here. Are you saying that because the two operations were so close in time together, you had no experience to drawn on for Storm, that you could have had from Flash? Is that how I should understand that statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Prosecutor. The point of my statement was to say that too little time had passed in order for us to draw any lessons from the similar situations that appeared after Operation Flash. So irrespective of the experience drawn from Flash, the government was not prepared to face new realities, at least not in operational terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have P462, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Skegro, I want to ask you briefly about three meetings. In each of these meetings, your name is not mentioned as one of the participants, and I have also done a word search for your name and do you not appear in the text of the meeting as having participated in the meeting. So I just want to ask if you remember being at the any of these meetings. The first one is an 11 August 1995 meeting, where -- with the president and others, where it was decided to pass the decree regarding the take-over of property that the Krajina Serbs left behind. Now, I understand that you probably have some knowledge of that decree and that law, but my question for you is: Were you present -- do you remember being present at that specific meeting where that decision was made?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: On the 11th of August, 1995, which was some five days after my visit to Knin, I was not in Zagreb. Therefore, I am not on the list of those present at the meeting. Are you trying to say that my name was omitted by mistake? I am afraid that I did not understand the gist of your question. Could you clarify please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question simply was, where Mr. Hedaraly said, Your name is not there. He more or less invites you to confirm that this was not by mistake but that you were not there, because there is always a possibility of a mistake. But you said you were not in Zagreb, so there is no suggestion in it in any way of taking out anything. Mr. Hedaraly is just seeking confirmation that where you do not appear that you also actually did not attend. Did you attend, did you not attend? I think from your answer, I took it, not being in Zagreb, that you confirm that you did not attend that meeting. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I was not in Zagreb. I was not at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The next one is P463, and this is a meeting where it appears that, from the cover page at least, that only President Tudjman and Dr. Radic are present. There is a discussion in there. One of the things being discussed is -- there's a statement made that not even 10 per cent of Serbs should return --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'll stay general. I'm not trying to argue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you try characterise that statement as precisely as possible, because you know that avoids that Mr. Kehoe remains on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to sit down now, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I am simply trying to provide based on the Chamber's guidance yesterday, and -- that's why I'm not going to talk about any areas, any specific parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But there's a -- do you remember being at the meeting where there is a statement made that not even 10 per cent of Serbs should return?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is simply -- if we turn to page 9 and 10 of 463, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 10 of the English, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, read it again, try to understand what Mr. Kehoe's problems are, and rephrase your question accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand what his problems are. I disagree with his characterisation, as I'm sure will not come as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- page 10. Could I have page 10 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It actually starts at the bottom of page 9, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will re-read it. Could we go to -- well, you can -- you can read English, Mr. Skegro. Why not invite the witness to read that portion so that he is aware what -- not to ask him to comment on it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If he remembers being present when that discussion took place. That's all I'm interested in, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is some discussion during this meeting, Mr. Skegro, about the return of Serb population. I leave it apart now, where exactly, what the exact number would have been, although 10 per cent has been mentioned. Does this ring in any way a bell as to your presence during that meeting; or would you say, I was not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was never present at any such meeting, but now I'm completely confused by the exchange between you, the Prosecutor, and Mr. Kehoe. I suppose that we are discussing the meeting that took place on the 22nd of August, 1995, and as can you read here, only two people were present, Dr. Jure Radic and President Tudjman. Is this what we are discussing at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is what we are discussing at the moment. And I take it from your answer that you say you were not present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am certain that I was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The last -- and once again, Mr. Skegro, I'm not suggesting that you were -- as the president said, I'm just seeking confirmation that you in fact were not, so if you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- for the next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, I will just explain it to you, because it -- sometimes if we have transcripts of meetings, sometimes people come and testify and say, Although my name is not here, I was present; or although my name is here, I was present but not during the whole of the meeting. Whereas it is always possible that someone is not mentioned on the cover page, but, nevertheless, says that he was in the room or in the room next to it, whatever varieties there are there life, that's the only reason why this is asked, to see whether what we find on paper, whether that is in accordance with your recollection. Nothing more, nothing less. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the last one of these I want to discuss or show you and ask you if you were present is the 20 -- is a 30 August meeting. And that is P466. And once again you will see your name is not present as the participants and it also does not appear in the rest of the document. And my question for you is: Do you remember a discussion about Serbs trying to return to Croatia via Hungary?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I was not at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skegro. Were you aware of a conversation that occurred between General Cermak and General Tolj regarding the crimes taking place in the aftermath of Operation Storm, and General Tolj telling General Cermak that there was pressure from -- he had pressure from higher up to say that it was civilians dressed in uniforms. Were you aware of such a conversation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I was not privy to that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few more questions but I'm about to change topics, so if we can -- I don't know if we want to have the break now. I can start now. There's a few documents that I want to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might be wiser to take the break first. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just briefly hear from the parties on the famous line to be translated. Let me be clear on one thing, first of all. That is, this document has been marked for identification, which means that if we want to -- the translation to be replaced, there's a formal procedure for that which will take -- we immediate to make a formal request to CLSS, it will then be checked. So, therefore, at this moment, we can't replace formally such a translation. At the same time, we -- it's a very practical matter that the witness will be gone by that time, and that, therefore, if there would be one way or another to get an indication from the parties, based on their information, whether they would consider it very likely or less likely that such a formal request would result in a different translation, I would like to hear from the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have discussed the matter with Mr. Cayley and we have both checked independently and both came -- received the same information, that -- I don't know if you want to pull it up on the screen so that we are clear, and it is P2640, page 71 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. While that -- you earlier said 71. In e-court it appears on page 70. And the number at the bottom of that page is 70 out of 120. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, then I'm sure it is still the same. My version said 71 out of 120, but I'm sure it doesn't change the -- now. And that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think it is -- it is the line --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- "and then a question arises here, President" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- "shall I go to Washington and lie to those people?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the line we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what the parties have come to a joint conclusion is that the -- it actually says: "And then a question arises here, President, shall I go now? I will not [Realtime transcript read in error "now"] lie to these people in Washington. If it is for the benefit of Croatia, I will lie to the Pope," and then it continues, and there's no dispute as to the remaining portion of that excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have to understand this portion, and now I'm addressing you as well, Mr. Skegro, that you said, If you send me to Washington I'll not lie; I may lie to the Pope, or I may have lied in the past but here I would not lie. That's the -- now, common understanding. Then we'll have to make a formal request for the translation to be verified, and we will then act from now on in this courtroom on the basis of the agreement between the parties of what this line says. Mr. Skegro, you see that any serious complaint about translation we'll deal with that, and you have followed the observations made by the parties and my observations, so that is now clear on the transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just on a technical matter, Mr. President. It is the Prosecution Exhibit so we have to make the request. Could we only make the request for that one sentence or for that one paragraph, or should we make -- it doesn't make sense to make a request for the entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the dispute is about the -- this sentence. Do we need to have the translation verified as well as to the other incidents of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- possible not speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You did also request that we look at the context in that particular paragraph falls and I think we would like, where we can agree on what additional pages would be put into evidence, that we would like all of those passages checked for accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is very reasonable, Mr. President. And we will agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the -- the context, as far as going to Washington and not to lie, that diminishes the relevance and importance of knowing exactly what the reason was, although we find that apparently on the further -- up on page 70, that we find some context. If you would please communicate with Mr. Hedaraly, which portions you would like to have verified exactly and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that he will follow your suggestions. Mr. Hedaraly, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have 65 ter 7424 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Skegro, what you will see on the screen is a -- is a report or portions of report from the Office of the Commissioner for Human Rights in Geneva discussing the media situation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I want to go on the second page of this document in the English, and I believe it's the -- also the beginning of the second page in the B/C/S. If we can go further down in the B/C/S, please. Thank you. And the top of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it says here, Mr. Skegro: "On 25 January 1996, in the parliament building, Mr. Skegro met Ms. Edita Vlahovic and, unsatisfied with her writings (Ms. Vlahovic wrote an article 'Skegro's Phenomenal Numbers,' in which she criticised new state budget) Skegro started to threaten her, You should be killed. After that he followed her to journalists' room and there (in front of several other journalists) took the pistol from one of the security guards, triggered it to her, asked, 'What do you say on this?' And after that, 'I will kill you now.' After that Skegro started to laugh and said it was just a joke." Mr. Skegro, can you tell us what exactly you thought was funny about pointing a gun at someone and telling them you would kill them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: It's not a funny matter. The only problem is that this never happened. This is a shameless lie, due to which I instituted legal proceedings, as did the journalist, and after three years of proceedings, there was a judgement acquitting me of any responsibility, but the newspapers that carried such lies were found guilty and had to publish a retraction and also pay a fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you ever threaten the journalist in any way, even without a gun, and saying that she should be killed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 7424 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we object. The reliability of this information has been challenged by the witness who said very clearly, This is a shameless lie, and there have even been legal proceedings as the journalist instituted as well. So even the subject matter of the issue and the basis of the question appears to have challenged this particular piece of information. In those circumstances we submit that it does not pass the reliability test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, what if we would have copies of those judgements, which give us a full view on what happened, also the reasoning of what the witness said about the courts concluding there was no blame for Mr. Skegro. However, that the journalists were even fined for -- I don't know exactly for what, but that seems to be the documentation which would support the answer of the witness and would give a full insight in what is reported here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, the Prosecution have not asked for that, Your Honour, and I feel that the obligation is being put on us like a burden of proof in relation to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Sometimes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- a matter that, in my submission, the witness has dealt with. If anyone wants to take it further and prove whatever issues, let them do so. But for my part, I don't want to have to spend time chasing matters that I don't think are of substance in relation to the issues in this trial, and I appreciate Your Honours' suggestion but I do have to draw a line in the sand on matters such as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber invites the parties to see before it calls for this evidence itself, which is -- the Chamber is entitled to do, to see whether these judgements are available, and if they are easily accessible, to see whether they can be produced; and, meanwhile, we'll MFI this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and we will obviously follow the Court's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps the witness could help us out. He apparently was -- do you have copies of those judgements because you said, I was totally -- well, I don't know ... you were acquitted or it's not entirely clear to me what kind of proceedings these were. But at least the court said that you were not to be blamed for anything; however, the journalists were. Do you have copies of those judgements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. I can send them to you, perhaps even today, by fax. If my wife can find them in our home archives. But you can also apply to the municipal or county courts in Zagreb, and they will send these judgements to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would be so kind to see whether can you -- because that goes far quicker, I take it, if you have copies available, to send it. And then the Chamber will consider whether it will be first given to the parties or whether the Chamber would like to have a look at it as well, at this moment. But, of course, it may shed further light on what is now tendered into evidence on the reliability of it -- of this document, and, at the same time, reliability and credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter. We note that no issues have been raised as to the provenance of this information, how this document came about, which I would have thought would have been important on a matter such as this. We've sort of gone straight to the issue, putting the Defence witness in the position of dealing with it without it being put on the maker of the statement, the responsibility to back up what is said, where this information came from, what this document is, which is why, in a way we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- opposing and have taken a line on -- on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, you earlier objected on the basis of reliability, mainly focussing on the answers the witness has given. Mr. Hedaraly, the document will be marked for identification. If you could provide further information or seek further information - perhaps the witness knows what the document is, where it comes from - and there's a lot of handwriting in it as well, what's the origin of this document, that would certainly assist the Chamber in later on deciding whether or not this is an admissible piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is a document that the Prosecution received from, as I mentioned, the office -- the High Commissioner for Human Rights as part of a larger, a much larger collection of documents, but hundreds of pages, and this is one -- one of the documents in that -- in that collection we received. As far as we know, the handwritten notes were how the documents were found in those archives when they were sent to us, and that is the information that we have regarding its provenance. And it -- that it was -- from the face of it, we see that it discusses the media situation and the freedom of the press issues and so on. That is the information I have for the Chamber on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we see already on the face of the document that it's -- the typewriting is in -- apparently in sections. Is there any information as to not only where it comes from, but also how they were produced, created, who takes responsibility for the -- for the text in it, and on what basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't have that information, and, Mr. President, it does -- I do agree with Your Honour and it does seem like it has been different sections collated together in one -- in one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know if the Prosecution has done any research on information they are putting and perhaps they can be asked about that, because we have just been on to a web site of Helsinki Watch which deals with the matter according to the -- what the witness has already said. That's on Sanction now. My Case Manager got it in one minute, and we can put it on for the Court to see if the Court wants to see that this instant. We're having to deal with something that is put up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should we put it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- use it in re-examination then. Because from the mere fact that I asked these questions to Mr. Hedaraly, of course, that is an expression of the relevance of finding answers to those questions before the Chamber finally decides whether or not to admit this MFI'd document. Any further matters, I would not at this moment interrupt the

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is there if the Court wanted to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we would invite to you do that in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. There's one matter as well which is of concern, the translation of the disputed sentence, transcript page 35, line 2. We have on our transcript, "I will now lie to these people in Washington," which I think we can all agree was not what Mr. Hedaraly said, in the joint submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The word "now" there seems to replace the word "not."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "I will not now," in fact, was the agreed statement between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I later summarised it in the sense --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which I think is now in agreement between the parties, and finally we'll get an official correction anyhow, because, as Mr. Hedaraly said, he will ask. After having consulted with Mr. Cayley, he will ask for a formal -- but you're perfectly right that on the transcript we find now a confusing statement. It has been corrected now. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With regard to the documents on the screen, I trust that the subject of discussion is simply the paragraph dealing with the witness in page 2. But the balance of the document is somewhat incendiary. Not somewhat, it is very incendiary, and, of course, we would object to any admission at any point regarding any of those issues because A, they have no relevance to these proceedings, but more importantly, we're not permitted to get to the provenance of this document and who is exactly making these allegations. So if we're going address this issue and it's going to be MFI'd, we would ask the Prosecution to redact every portion of that document expect that portion that they are trying to admit into evidence, which I trust is the paragraph beginning: "On 25 May 1996."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I take it that you want to focus on the portion you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, and that was 25 January, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is January -- sorry, 25 January 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY BUT --
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skegro. Let me show you another article from a newspaper and another allegation made against you, and I will ask you to comment on that. It's 65 ter 7421. It's an article from the Independent Newspaper, dated 1 November 2000. It discusses the tapes of these presidential meetings. We've seen some of these transcripts here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And once it comes up on the screen, I will ask to please go to the second page in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY BUT --
utterances.text: And I want to focus on the second paragraph in the English, which is the third paragraph in the B/C/S, and the Independent writes: "One set of tapes show how Tudjman and his cronies skim 100 million (69 million pounds) off the top of a near billion-dollar selloff of Croatia's telephone service. Some of the money went into a political slush fund. "On the afternoon of 13 October last year, Tudjman met with the then deputy prime minister and finance minister Borislav Skegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKEGRO SAID
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've put the money aside for December because I think we need it. We have to prepare for the upcoming elections. He added: It's in an Irish bank ... 100 per cent safe. Only you and I know about this." Mr. Skegro, can you comment on this? Were you aware of that allegation being made and can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. Prosecutor, but I think it would be more much effective for this Honourable Chamber to get a hold of transcript of my alleged conversation with Mr. Tudjman rather than this source, which is a description of this conversation. If you were to get a hold of the original transcript, you would see it was a perfectly legitimate conversation between the president and a minister of finance of a country discussing where legitimate funds were deposited and were also discussing how other ministers were not aware of the existence of that money; otherwise, as ministers are prone to do, they would have spent that money already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY BUT --
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skegro. I haven't shown you the transcript. Unfortunately, I don't have it. We will definitely ask for it and look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In the meantime, Your Honour, if we could have that exhibit tendered or marked for identification as well as the previous one, which was 65 ter 7424, for which we did not receive a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, first, we'll ask for a number -- an MFI number for the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, reminds me that the word "last" is confusing me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 07424 becomes Exhibit P2642, marked for identification; and 65 ter number 07421 becomes Exhibit P2643, also marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Any objections against admission of the publication on the -- well, let's say the -- the amount of money in the Irish bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Because it has not been adopted by the witness and he asked that, If you have got information to put to me about it that directly from the source, show it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, again, we have another document that has made incendiary allegations where we can't back to the provenance of those allegations. That's number one. Number two, what is the relevance of a conversation that is taking place in 1999? I haven't heard any articulated relevance on that score. Certainly it is outside the scope of this indictment. It simply doesn't fit squarely within any evidence that we have. This article itself is 1 November 2000, and if I'm not mistaken, and I can be corrected, this is apparently relaying a conversation of 13 October 1999. For all of the above-stated reasons, A, the incendiary nature of it, which we can't get to the core of the -- even the writer of this; two, we don't have the actual tape to see exactly what transpired; and three, it's outside of the scope of the indictment and completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, could I invite to you especially respond to the relevance also in view of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, first of all, we have had discussions of newspaper articles numerous times and when the person is mentioned in it, it has typically gone to the weight to be accorded to the document and not its admissibility. Second of all, our submission would be that such allegations square -- fall squarely within Rule 90(H), and its relevance is the credibility of the witness that is testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may respond to that, Judge, and I would test the statement by the Prosecution. When the Prosecution presents evidence that was completely outside the time-frame of this indictment, ergo irrelevant, as opposed to a commentary by a witness talking about events that took place during the time-frame of this indictment, clearly, for the plain reading of this document is we're talking about a conversation where we don't have the underlying document that is in the latter part of 1999, years after the time-frame of this indictment and clearly irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I mean, if -- just briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First -- before -- Mr. Kay, do you have any -- is there any need for you to further respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No need -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If the allegations are correct, it shows dishonesty. If it shows dishonesty, it affects the credibility of the witness and therefore is clearly relevant. Although not the underlying facts may not be relevant to this indictment, but the evidence would be relevant to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, one last --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, it -- it -- obviously this witness has been known by the Prosecution to come for some time. If this is such an important issue concerning this witness's credibility, the Chamber deserves what the context of this conversation is, and not have some statement concerning any witness's credibility thrown out with the hopes that it's somehow going to -- to smear or -- or put some type of dark stain on evidence coming in. But be that as it may, it's simply so far outside the scope of this indictment it simply has no relevance.
