Now, if we were to engage in a media search of every witness that discussed things throughout the entire time-frame of this person's life or space of time that they were in office, I'm sure we could find a lot of things. That's not the purpose of what this Trial Chamber has to do, which is to find out what the facts are and make decisions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you look at the transcript, page 47, line 3, it reads: "Mr. Kehoe, one last," and then I wanted to say "line," which would certainly have guided you not to take 15 lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, just for the record, the Markac Defence is standing along the arguments of my learned colleagues of other two Defences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The document will be marked for identification. Mr. Registrar, we -- or have you -- you have given it a number already, yes, and then I asked -- so that's -- it has been marked. Yes, P2643. We'll further consider admissibility of these documents. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Kay, when I'm asking you where there's any need to re-examine the witness, it's also in a bit of an expectation that you would take us to the Internet and to find out what happened with the story of the threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'll just explain the source of the Internet we're looking at. Helsinki Watch Human Rights, and if the passage can be found. Put it on Sanction, please. I'm in between two experts, Your Honour and I'm not quite sure who is driving the car. I suppose I'm supposed to be driving the car, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when you said that you could find it in one minute I thought that you were praising your team members. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, we had it in actually less, and I think the Court can see on the screen: "On the 26th of July, the vice-president of the Croatian government, Borislav Skegro threatened Edita Vlahovic working for Novi List with a gun which he had taken from a security officer at the parliament building. Legal proceedings were initiated against Skegro, but he was acquitted on all counts."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Skegro? That's just a report we have pulled up. And would you like to elaborate any further on the matter beyond that paragraph we have been able to find there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to correct some things. It was not on the 22nd -- 26th of July, but 22nd of January. But this is neither here nor there. It was not the parliament building but the government building. So these are technicalities. And the rest is correct, that I was acquitted of all charges and not only that. At the same time I sued the papers that conveyed the lies and those were the weekly, Globus, and the dailies, Glas Slavonije and Novi List. And I won all the three suits and was compensated for damages. So it was -- the parties appealed and the cases went to a higher instance court, which was a county court, where my innocence was again confirmed. They appealed at the Supreme Court, and four or five years later, from the beginning of the proceedings, the appeals court confirmed the original sentence, and that was that the document that was purportedly conveyed was nothing but a blatant lie. Now what happened and why it happened, I believe that we could organise a parallel trial in order to investigate and establish what actually happened and why it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The information that you gave us there as to what took place over this matter, was that reported in the Croatian media?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. However, if somebody is charged with crimes, then the titles appear in three-inch block letters. And when that same journalist has to deny the original article after the court decision, then that appears on page 57 of the same newspaper, in a very, very small letters, in font 3 letters. I'm talking about the size of the letters when I say font 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And questions I want to ask you about is, because you were put an extract from some document or other, but how freely available, if someone had researched this matter and looked for the public details to check them, how easy that would have been today in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I really don't know how available documents are in court archives and whether you can access documents on complete cases. I would assume that it shouldn't be difficult. But I repeat, I had the original of the final decision at home, where it says, expresses verbis expressly everything that shows that the allegations against me were lies. The journalist herself, before the Trial Chamber, at the express question, whether this happened, she said no, did he say this and that, and she replied, No, he didn't. So, sapienti sat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And those details you've told us about, that the journalist involved in this particular matter, was that reported in the media and press, if anyone had looked that up, taken the time to research the matter?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe if you Google my name, her name, and the word "court decision," I'm sure you will find some results. But apart from the Google, there's some official archives, which in my view are the only relevant ones, and I'm sure that they would be much better to use. That lady was also a victim. She was also set up just like I was. She was not the one who initiated the whole matter and who actually launched the allegations against me. I have a question. I don't have the text, the English text of the transcript of my words on the screen. I would very much like to have the transcript on the screen, the transcript of my words, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This the document marked for identification, which was -- yeah, P2642. Is that the one you wanted to see or did you want to see the -- the document we put on the -- the one with words is in the extract that the -- of the document the Prosecution produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that coming up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now have I everything that I need. I have the LiveNote on the left screen, which is brilliant, and I have the document, the relevant document on the right-hand side screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you want to look at those words again and make a comment?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: No. No, it is self-explanatory. You can see that this was a copy/paste exercise, five-size font, somebody throwing words at somebody else. But the essence of the matter was contained in my previous answer. It really does not matter very much what the provenance of the document is. What matters are the facts of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just as a general matter, is this a -- a usual or unusual conflict between a public figure in Croatia, such as yourself, and -- and the media?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, every time that was not a -- the only one or an unusual case. Of course, this was the most difficult and serious incident in my career, an allegation that appeared in a weekly, and then it was blown out of proportion in all the dailies that are mentioned here. And when the inertia took hold, I had to fight against the windmills. And when it -- the matter came to the court, it was not easy to prove my innocence. It was just like the indictment against Socrates which was so absurd that it cannot -- it could simply not be refuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You heard the statement by the Prosecution that they were asking questions based on issues of credibility, and as a result, I want to ask you this. Is the statement that you have made in this court, in relation to these proceedings, the truth?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Any ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skegro, I wanted to ask you questions -- a question regarding your statement in paragraph 8. You are mentioning normalisation included the return of persons displaced in 1991 as well as those who left homes in 1995 for all regardless of their ethnic affiliations. We had and we -- it was already admitted into evidence also this transcript between president and Radic, where numbers of possible return of displaced Serbs was mentioned, and it was mentioned not more than 10 per cent. My question is to you: Do have you some knowledge whether government implemented such a tacit agreement in the practical way?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm stating that the government never implemented, planned or intended to implement a discrimination of this kind. What we can discuss here is what was relevant at any given moment, which refugees were capable of returning and which were not. What I'm saying is that in 1991, first Croats were expelled and then continued to live in refugee camps in hotels and all over the place, and they also were supposed to return. So we're not talking only about the programme for the return of the Serbs. We are also talking about the programme for the return of the Croats as well, of everybody, to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: I understand, excuse me, Mr. Skegro but I just wanted to know this in brief answer. And next question is to me: If government decided or governmental authorities or civil servants decided to adopt a programme, for instance, was there such situations that Mr. Tudjman would effect this decision and simply revoke it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to be absolutely sure that I understand your question properly in order to be able to provide a proper answer. You are asking me if the government could make a decision and then President Tudjman would use his authority to overturn or change that decision. Did I understand your question correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: A thing of that kind never happened. It could not have happened. It would not have been based on law. President Tudjman did not have the authority to overthrow a decision by the government or the parliament. He cannot just simply override a decision by any of the two bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And last question from me is, in paragraph 9 you mentioned that that situation, financial -- at that time financial situation was very tense. And my question is to you: Do you have some knowledge how Mr. Cermak's authority and jobs what he was conducted was financed at that time? Which was financing sources by -- it was paid by military budgets or it was paid by civilian budget and -- or did he have some separate bookkeeping system?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: To be honest, Your Honour, I don't know. I should have to rewind, go back in time and try to deduct conclusions from the system as it functioned. I suppose that some of the funds were allocated from the budget of the government, some from the military budget, but I really wouldn't be able to explain how this was done. I can't provide a precise answer. Maybe you should ask Mr. Cermak. I'm sure that he would be able to answer that much better than I -- than I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for those answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. First of all, I would like to come back to these judgements, I would really appreciate if you could find them and ... Now, the -- counsel for Mr. Cermak drew attention to the matter of the journalist by taking us to the International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights annual report 1997, because, Mr. Kay, I checked that on the Internet to see the context of what was shown to us. Now, the issue there is raised in a context of criticism to the way in which the Penal Code was used against journalists rather than as primary serving to demonstrate that you were acquitted. That's the reason why I would very much like to see that -- that judgement. Now, if you say you were acquitted, or at least that's what the report says and what you said, was there a trial, or was the case dismissed before trial?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a trial, which, in different stages, lasted for three years. There were three different judges and three separate proceedings, which dealt with the same subject. Why three? Well, that's Croatian judiciary for you. In one proceedings, the journalist sued me for a death threat. Because, if what the newspapers published was true, then it would have been logical to expect she sued me for that, and I was fully acquitted on all counts. She lost and, you know, it happened as I've told you. In the second proceedings, I sued the second and third newspaper which conveyed these uncritical texts and lies about me, referring to the first newspapers. And in each of those subsequent articles, they added on something, which wasn't present in the initial article. So, I will forward you the copies of these judgements, Your Honour, with great pleasure, but in view of the entire situation and the cooperation with The Hague, I don't know what the right channels are. Should I just simply put in an envelope and mail it to the ICTY in The Hague or should I do it via some office in Croatia for cooperation with the ICTY? I think it would be best if this entire matter was resolved in this way, rather than searching on Internet and conveying who heard wrongly this or that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you may have been aware of, I was very much in favour of looking at the original documents. I don't think, as a matter of fact, that these are all public judgements. I take it that there's no confidentiality involved in any way and therefore, I see no problem in it being sent to the Tribunal directly.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: That's how I will do it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll check that, once we have received it. Since you are here now, I have, nevertheless, have one additional question for you. When you say you were acquitted after having been at trial, was it established that a gun was used but it was not to be taken as a threat; or that you never, ever had a gun in your hands; or is it -- I mean, an acquittal can take various forms. Could you tell us which form it took, as far as facts were concerned?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can certainly tell you this. Number one, I never, ever had a gun in my hands. Number two, yes, a security person was pointing to a gun in his hands. Number three, yes, I was present in that room at that particular moment, together with the journalist. And this is a room adjoining the room where the government meeting was to be held, and all of this was taking place just immediately prior to the beginning of the meeting, and there's live broadcast for journalists to follow the proceedings. And I arrived there some five minutes earlier in order to have a cigarette there. Several days later, in an unsigned text written by a person who was not present, these terrible accusations emerged. Later on, I realised that it wasn't by accident, it wasn't by chance, it wasn't an innocent mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, most important for me is to know what we will find in the judgement. We will find this information all in the judgement you --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: That's correct. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask Mr. Registrar to tell the Victims and Witness Section to give you an address where you can send these documents. Your statement says that you -- when you were driving through the area, that you wondered who would have put on fire houses, that you discussed that, and who would have done that. Were you aware of allegations that the Croatian military were involved in putting houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: At that time, Your Honours, you actually go back to my statement, where I describe how we travelled through Korenica, right? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: At that point in time, no. Just like it says in my statement, we could see on the side sheep that had been killed. We could conclude that it was done by automatic weapons, which is something that is not normal. This was 20 or 30 metres from the main road, this flock of sheep. One could see smoke rising in the distance; obviously something was on fire. Naturally at that point in time, I didn't know. Later on, information emerged, people learned of things, evidence was collected, and in order to reply to your question, whether this was done by members of the Croatian Army, I cannot tell you anything but, yes, this has been done by people in uniforms. What capacity they acted in, what were they, were they just camouflaged robbers, demilitarised members of Croatian Army who went on a rampage in order to avenge something, I don't know, Your Honours. We would really have to examine this on a case-by-case basis. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of paragraph 14 of your statement you say: "The Croatian Army and police were issuing orders to prevent looting and arson." Do you have any detailed knowledge of it? I mean, what's the source of this part of your statement.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am afraid I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my question -- your statement again reads in this respect, and I'll put it in context. You said: "I was concerned then that with police forces which we had at our disposal we could not successfully cover such a large territory which was suddenly free. Operation Storm took place several months after Operation Flash, and we had no experience. The RH government tried to get prosecutors and courts to start working as soon as possible. The police were doing their job. We were trying to remove the army from the town. The Croatian Army and the police were issuing orders to prevent looting and arson." What I wanted to know is your familiarity with such orders, apparently what was undertaken, what your knowledge was about the police doing their jobs. How did you follow these events, and what -- on what factual basis you stated that the Croatian Army and the police were issuing orders to prevent looting and arson? Did you see those orders? Who exactly issued them? Could you tell us more about the details of this portion of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I have understood your question now. Thank you, Your Honour. I was a member of the government, of the cabinet, which met at least twice a week during that period of time. Naturally, the first and main points on our agenda were matters that had to do with normalisation, report from the ground, as we called them, whether it was the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Justice, or Ministry of the Interior. Who informed on this, which is to say that a member of the government under whose responsible this was not directly. So that was my primary source of information. As for the rest, any of us can gather information, based on something they heard, they read, and so on, but in this particular case I based this exclusively on the reports received at government cabinet meetings. And I think that in your documentation you must have documents and minutes from the meetings of the Croatian cabinet which quite clearly and unambiguously say who needs to do what in order for the situation to improve, because the situation, as it was, was not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. One final question. When Mr. Cermak was appointed earlier on as a minister, we find in your statement that it was meant to an appointment only for a relatively limited period of time. When Mr. Cermak was appointed in 1995 as garrison commander, it was also he served there for a limited portion of time. Could you tell us, do you know of any reason why these appointments would be only for such a short period of time? I'm just wondering ...

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak is present here. He would probably be better placed to answer your first question. I suppose that he wanted to come out of the government establishment and those bodies and go into private business. Your Honours, there were a lot of us in that government who were in the role, I will use a German word for you, Gastarbeiter there. We were not professional politicians. It's just that we were invited by President Tudjman, in those early days of the creation of the state, to contribute in roles which were not our true roles that we intended to play for the rest of our lives. I spent eight years in the government and Mr. Cermak and I both went back to our previous domain which was private business. So I suppose that was his primary motivation. As for the second matter, I think that we can suppose that by definition this was a transitional role, when, after the army had played its role, the civilian authorities need to be established in an area where, I emphasise once again, the Croatian government did not have control over for five years. So not a single office, not a single service, not a single body where you could go and obtain some documents existed within the system of the Republic of Croatia. And this lasted since August 1990, that is to say, five years prior to Operation Storm. So in that sense, by definition this role of Mr. Cermak was to be transitional and short -- of short limitation, until regular authorities were established and could take over their regular duties as defined by law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My last question to you is the following. This Chamber has heard quite some evidence about an incident that took place in the village of Grubori in the last few days of August 1995. Did you learn anything about this incident, or did you not hear anything about it at that time? I'm not asking you for further details and what you know about it, but whether you, at all, got acquainted with such a thing that had happened.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes. I became aware and that place remained etched in my memory as a place where a terrible crime had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, where did you learn about this event?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: At the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was discussed at a cabinet meeting or ...

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Your Honours, despite all my efforts, I cannot remember any details. But I know that it was discussed at the government gatherings. Now, I know I discussed it with Nikica Valentic. Now whether it was at preparatory meetings, official cabinet meetings, whether it was in his office, I really couldn't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was at the time when it happened, just to have a time-frame for your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, several days after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you describe it as -- and let me repeat your words. You describe it as a terrible crime. What, as far as you know, was done about that crime? Because you told us that the police were doing their job.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I suppose that relevant bodies did their job, the police, the prosecutor's office, along the lines of how the justice system was established in those days. When I said that I heard that a terrible crime had taken place, according to what I heard, there was a group of the elderly who were killed practically in their homes by somebody. Now, as to who did it, how they did it, Your Honours, I don't know that to this day, let alone back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was discussed in terms of crime, rather than as an incident. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, you understood me well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you did not learn about this incident as being part of any combat activities. Is that also correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it, because this had allegedly happened several days after main combat operations had been completed. But it's hard for me now to speculate about the details after all these years. Your Honours, it is hard for me to discern what I learned at the -- at that particular moment and what I learned subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But whether you learned it subsequently or not, this is what you learned, what you told us?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Mr. Kay, have the questions by the Bench triggered --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any need to further examine the witness. Mr. Kay may have some further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, you referred to meetings took place by the cabinet in answer to His Honour's questions about orders being given in relation to crimes. At those meetings you refer to, would Mr. Jarnjak, the minister for the Ministry of Interior, was he present?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: At some of them. At the cabinet meetings, of course, either Minister Jarnjak, or, if Minister Jarnjak was not available, then he would have his deputy replacing him at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the name of the deputy, if Mr. Jarnjak wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: You're putting my memory at test. I believe that his deputy was Mr. Gledec. I say "deputy" but I'm not 100 per cent sure. I was vice-president of the government for a long time, and during that time, there was a time when Gledec was Jarnjak's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And also, in relation to the same meetings, was the minister for the Ministry of Defence, Mr. Susak, present?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes. Either Susak personally or, again, his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just for the record, the name of the deputy?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, that was Mr. Kresimir Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've had discussion about the media report of this incident with the journalist. I'd like you to just look at another report, which can deal with the matter very quickly on Sanction, from the HINA news agency. And if you could just read out what you see there. Remember to do it slowly so that the translators can translate. First of all, the headline?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: The headline: "Skegro acquitted of charges." And in the heading -- I can read actually the same. Is that what you wanted me to go -- start reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: In the text, the body of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The text, the body of the text.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: "The municipal court in Zagreb acquitted the vice-president of the government, Borislav Skegro, of charges from a civil suit by the journalist of Novi List, Edita Vlahovic Zuvela. According to the charges, at the beginning of last year, on the 26th of January, he threatened journalist Vlahovic with a gun and insulted her on account of an article which was entitled: "Phenomenal figures," produced by Borislav Skegro, that was published in the Novi List of Rijeka. "In the statement of reasons of the acquittal, Judge Marin Mrcela stated that the court did not find any proof that Skegro had committed the acts that he was charged with, and the Trial Chamber also said that the decision was reached based on the credibility of the statements by the witness, Based on the credible statements, I believe that it was not established that Borislav Skegro ever held a gun. I believe that it was not established that he ever threatened journalist Vlahovic that he would kill her, and I believe that it was not established that he ever called her a murderer with a baby face. That was said on Wednesday by Judge Mrcela, when the -- the decision was delivered. Journalist Edita Vlahovic has right to appeal against the municipal court judgement to the county court. HINA on 29th of September, 2009."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's today's date, because this has been downloaded. Thank you very much for that. You've been asked to forward the judicial documents to the Court. For that we're grateful. Can you check that you forward all relevant documents, including the appeal, anything in the nature of these judgements, to the Court?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I will do that. I'm sure that I have the first-instance court judgement, the second-instance court judgement. I will send you whatever I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my questions of the matters arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may, very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skegro, His Honour asked you about the incident in the village of Grubori and you said that you remember that that matter was discussed at the government session, and that the incident was, indeed, discussed. At any of the government sessions, did you ever discuss the incidents, in terms of this incident being ignored or hushed down, or was the contrary said, the -- and that is that the incident had to be investigated by the authorised bodies. Can you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Not only at the session of the government but also during the consultations by the members of the government, there was never any reference to the incident being ignored or hushed down. It was just the contrary. There were requests for investigation and there were also requests for the culprits to be punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, did it ever happen that at any of the sessions of the government you received information that there had been attempts to hush down the event or influence the investigation into the incident that had taken place in the village of Grubori?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, I would like to ask you whether or not you recall an incident in -- in and about October or September of 1995, in some killing allegations from Varivode. Do you recall that? And do you recall it being discussed at cabinet meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that Varivode and Grubori were the two names of the villages or hamlets that I had not been familiar with before that, and that all of a sudden turned up, as major, major problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was -- I was just wondering how that had arisen from the Bench's questions. There was something about orders, there was something about Grubori. I don't remember Varivode or other crimes being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we've now heard the answer of the witness, that at least Varivode was a name that -- that he became familiar with at the time. Mr. Kehoe, any response to what Mr. Hedaraly raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will gladly give the response outside the presence of the witness. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- foretell that particular statement. But I will gladly talk about that. The problem with this witness, of course, is this witness speaks English as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, my next question will clearly show the relevance. I don't think we need to send the witness out, but I think my next question will put it on the table at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put your next question to the witness, whether we will ask him to answer that question is then a matter possibly for discussion and then in the absence of the witness. Please put the question. And, Mr. Skegro, you are invited not yet to answer the question that Mr. Kehoe will put to you before I have invited you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, with regard to these conversations in cabinet meetings and outside cabinet meetings that you were talking about, could it that be you that are confusing the Varivode incident which was discussed at cabinet meetings with Grubori? Could you be confusing those two incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kehoe, can you be more specific about the period? If you're asking whether I heard about Varivode and Grubori during the month of September 1995, then I really can't tell you with any degree of certainty that I heard of the both at that time. If you are asking me whether that was sometime towards the end of 1995, then I could probably say yes. Before the end of 1995, I heard of both places, but I believe that you have too high expectations of me at the moment. It is possible that I heard of Varivode subsequently, which means maybe not one, two, or five days after the incident that had taken place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Following up with that, Mr. Skegro, there's evidence on the record that there is discussion in cabinet meetings with Minister Jarnjak and other officials in October of 1995 regarding the Varivode incident. Now, with that evidence that is before this Trial Chamber being presented by the Office of the Prosecutor, my question to you is: Given that fact, which is undisputed in the record, could you confusing the discussions of killing incidents that took place in the cabinet meetings and confusing the Varivode incident which was discussed with Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly. Before you answer that question, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Kehoe asked that question already and the witness answered. Second of all, it's page 61 of today's transcript in answer to -- the question was very clear from Your Honour that it was the last few days of August and the witness's answer was clear that that place remained etched in his memory. So I think that should also in fairness be put to the witness; otherwise Mr. Kehoe is not liking the answer gave the first time and asking him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Well, I object to the counsel's speeches. I object to the speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kehoe, when I give an opportunity to Mr. Hedaraly, then let me just take one second. I'd like to invite the witness to leave the courtroom for a second, so that we can follow up the objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It might be a moment to take the break, so to speak, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, at the same time it might well be that we could finish within the next five or seven minutes, in which case it would be not a good idea to have the witness wait for another half an hour. Would you please follow the usher for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let me put a few matters together. I asked the witness about his knowledge of an incident which appears in the indictment and whether this was how he obtained acknowledge of that. I only mentioned the name of the village, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the time, Judge. You put the time in there of August. He didn't put the time in, Your Honour, you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to come to that. What I meant to say is that I didn't say anything about what the event was. I only relate to Grubori. Then I'd given him the time and I asked him for a time-frame when he learned about it. He said, Just a couple of days after the event. I specifically asked for that. Which situates us somewhere in either late August or early September. The witness describes the incident himself, spontaneously, as elderly killed more or less in their homes. Now, to put to the witness all kind of evidence on when the Varivode matter was discussed and say, Wouldn't you be confused, could also induce confusion in certainty, which is, in view of the questions I raised with the witness about an incident which he describes, whether it was a clear time-frame, might not, in every respect, serve the finding of the -- the facts. Before the Chamber decides on whether or not we will allow you to continue your line of questioning, I thought it would be fair to give you an opportunity and to give Mr. Hedaraly an opportunity to comment on what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you asked this witness the time-frame, he's not going to give a specific recollection of the time-frame. In evidence is D214. It is a -- the minutes of a cabinet meeting of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. -- that's not the issue. I asked him about late August. And he said he learned about it a couple of days after that. What happened in October, that's not -- I think is not contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President, with all due respect. It is contested because the witness is conflating two issues that were discussed in cabinet meetings. These Varivode incident, which, Judge, does involve killing of elderly people in their homes, does -- was discussed at a cabinet meeting in October of 1995. And we go do D214. One of the deputy prime ministers present, the first name mentioned after Valentic, is in fact Mr. Skegro. He is at that meeting when they are discussing that killings at Varivode, which involve - I don't want to say the same facts of Grubori - but a parallel case where there are killings of elderly people. Now, the issue here is the possible merger of these particular incidents in a man who is asked about this some nine years -- or excuse me, some 14 years after the fact. Now, those are issues that are pertinent because why we talk about an incident in Varivode that is discussed where in fact the government did do something about it. Where we -- we have a discussion about it that it is out in the open and that is the reason why we are going into it. Now this is cross-examination. And I do believe that in cross-examination we're entitled to test this witness's recollection about particular events, and that's all I'm trying to do is get some clarity as to exactly what's discussed at this cabinet meeting. And if in fact I put to him this -- that matter which is in the record already, the discussion of Varivode in the cabinet meeting, if that calls into some question his memory and recollection concerning a discussion regarding Grubori that took place in a cabinet meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I -- I don't really have any further submissions, Your Honour. He asked the question, the witness answered, and now Mr. Kehoe wants to educate him and show him more documents to get the conclusion that he wants. But we leave it in the Chamber's hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, with some hesitation, the Chamber will allow you to put further questions to the witness in this respect. At the same time, whether the Rules for whether this is real cross-examination, that is, examining the witness on matters that were asked by the calling party, that is still a matter to be seen, because the matter had not been raised in any way. At the same -- therefore, the Chamber, in order to be best assisted by the testimony of the witness, would expect you to -- to be very cautious in inducing to the witness -- this witness is an intelligent person, and it's easy to understand what confusion that may have arisen. The Defence would -- would not be negative for the Defence, if that confusion would arise, and that's -- might create dilemmas for the witness, so, therefore, you're invited to limit the signals of what is the preferred answer. I'm very cautious in saying this, and it has to do with a rather uncommon situation, that it's not normal -- it's not normal cross-examination, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe I -- I believe I understand Your Honours' guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is, if you push too hard on what was discussed at another moment, then if would you ask me, rather, receive spontaneous answers from the witness, if he has any hesitations I might instruct him to also express any hesitations he may have on certain matters. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I might just have two -- one or two questions to start with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, we talked before we asked you to leave the courtroom for a while, we talked about the Grubori incident, we talked about the Varivode incident. Could you characterise what you remember the Varivode incident was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really can't say anything, or, rather, not much more than the fact that when I heard about the incident, it seemed that somebody on the Croatian side allegedly committed a crime over the Serb civilians who had remained living in the area. This is the best I can do. I can't tell you who, when. It's very difficult to tell me anything about that. It was difficult at the time, and it is even more difficult today. But this is, that is, clearly on my mind. The Varivode and Grubori incidents -- or, rather, Varivode and Grubori as places where crimes took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you earlier answered a question, one of my questions about the Grubori incident, you were a bit more specific. You said elderly people killed in or approximately -- in their homes. Now, Varivode, could you give us a first characterisation of what you remember of that to be? Was it the same, was it different? How could you distinguish between the two in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, Your Honours, let's start with Grubori. I can't say that at the time I did not have precise information, or, rather, that at the time, which was a few days after the incidents in Grubori had taken place, that I had a full picture and that I knew that the persons involved were elderly people. Subsequently, and I can only speculate on when it was, a year, five or ten years later, I was provided with some details. It was relayed by the media, maybe in relation to the -- these trials here. It is very difficult for me to tell you when I heard the details of that incident for the first time. And as for Varivode, all that I remember is the name of the place where some sort of crime took place. Who was charged with the crimes, what happened, really, I can't remember. Maybe I can provide a third explanation. What you remember is names or some pairs of names, for example, Skabrnja, Vukovar; Srebrenica, Omarska; Varivode, Grubori. As to when you heard about any of them, what you learned about any of them, in my case it would take a lot of effort to say something before this Court under the oath and with full responsibility. I would really not go into any further details, because that would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you told us about the elderly, elderly people being killed approximately in their homes. Now, how did -- do you remember how you know that it was about elderly people being killed? Was that discussed in the meeting; did you see that from the media? What was the -- how did you get to know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, with the caveat that I'm trying very hard to remember. As for the people being elderly, I'm sure that I heard that much, much later, much later than August or September 1995, and I believe that I heard that within the context of The Hague indictments, because there was a lot said in the Croatian media about the crimes alleged in the indictments, the locations, or maybe I heard it in the reports of different NGOs that were active in Croatia. If you are asking me when it was when I learned that people were elderly for the first time, I really can't say. Today, as I sit here, I believe that they were elderly and now if you're asking me for a precise answer as to what happened and where and when it happened, I really can't be of much assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your last answer, you said again that, as you said before, that it was a couple of days after the incident that it was discussed. Is that the recollection that it was said this happened a couple of days before, or did you learn about the incident and then remember that a couple of days after that, that the meeting was held where the matter was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I assumed that when I first heard about the matter that we're discussing at the moment, it did not have to necessarily be tied with reference to specific names. For example, let me illustrate that by relaying a story to you when Prime Minister Valentic in the presence of some other ministers, told us that he was privy to information that we were not privy to at the time, because he received information from other services than us in the economy, and he said, We -- we know that a lot was going on in the liberated areas, that crimes were happening. He did not mention any names. He never mentioned the names of Grubori or Varivode, for example. That's my illustration of the point that I'm trying to bring home here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember that both of these incidents were discussed at meetings of the cabinet or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when? When were they discussed? Immediately after it -- we learned of it or they learned in the government about them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to that, I can't be certain that I was present in a meeting where it was discussed in detail, where information was provided about specific locations. So it's very difficult for me to pin-point time-wise when I learned of a crime in general, which happened in a liberated area in the vicinity of Knin, and when I learned the details concerning name of the village, kind of victims, suspects, and so on. It's very hard for me to discern that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You twice answered that it was a couple of days after the Grubori incident that it was discussed. You gave that answer twice. What I'm asking now is whether you also discussed the Varivode incident, and whether you have any recollection as to how much time that was after that event had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certain when it comes to Varivode that I cannot -- that I didn't know with precision about that place. What I'm trying to say, Your Honour, is the names of locations where a crime had happened were not important to me. It was the crimes that mattered to me. Now you're going into details of something that happened 14 years ago, and you're asking me to remember on which day I heard about a certain village, and I think that you are overestimating my memory and my abilities in that sense, especially since this was discussed and written about at length in the media for the last ten years. And, now, to ask me at what time I heard in detail about these incidents is something that I simply cannot give you an answer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, any further questions? I bring to your attention that the tape gives us only a couple of minutes, very few minutes, so if we would have to spend more time on it, then we would have to take another break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would suggest a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll, then, take the break first. We'll have a break and resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, I would like to have you take a look at a document that's in evidence. D214.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can bring that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, this is a -- the minutes of a closed session of the government of the Republic of Croatia dated 5 October 1995, before Prime Minister Valentic. As can you see from the list of deputy prime ministers, your name is first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would like to turn to page 8 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I will tell you, Mr. Skegro, based on the evidence in the record. And, specifically, Mr. President, D808, the incident in Varivode, took place on the 28th of September, 1995. This meeting being 5 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could just take it to the next page, I believe ... If we can go to the next page in the B/C/S, please. Scroll a little -- that's it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Skegro, this is a report that was presented by Minister Jarnjak. And Minister Jarnjak, in the second paragraph, also informed -- excuse me. That: "Jarnjak informed the government of the killing of nine Serb civilians in the village of Varivode, near Knin, noting that the all the civilians were elderly than they had been killed by fire-arms. I. Jarnjak also informed the government of the measures that the Ministry of the Interior had taken to find the perpetrators of this crime as quickly as possible. "After a date in which" -- several ministers, including yourself, Mr. Skegro, "took part, the government entrusted the Ministry of the Interior with regularly reporting to the government on all measures taken and the findings of the investigating bodies." Now, sir, given the fact that Varivode took place on the 28th of September, this meeting is 5 October, do you recall this discussion?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: Now that I see these minutes, then, yes. I remember, we talked about. Now whether I had heard about Varivode before this meeting or then, I don't know. But it is here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you get additional information on this incident, and as -- Grubori, as time went on?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV SKEGRO
utterances.text: I suppose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions to be put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skegro, since there are no further questions for you, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Skegro out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to deal with the whole of the MFI list, but there was a pending issue on orders by Mr. Mladic. There was some discussion about whether they were exculpatory, yes or no. Mr. Misetic announced that he would tender them from bar table, and I think we're still waiting for -- I don't think that numbers have already been assigned to them, Mr. Misetic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, there would be some consultations and that the Prosecution would express its views on whether it would oppose against these documents tendered in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe we've had correspondence back and forth and, Mr. President, we have received the comments from the Prosecution which we will incorporate into the spreadsheet that we have prepared, and I think that resolves the Prosecution's review, and I believe we can then tender them into evidence. But we have been privately communicating back and forth about the wording of the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's good that I'm not familiar with that. That's then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless there's any urgent procedural -- Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to inform Your Honours and Defence teams that it is Mr. Russo's last day today in the court and in the ICTY tomorrow, and since he was a very active participant in these proceedings, I just wanted to let you know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that I speak of all that we'll miss him. He's blushing a bit. That's not what he's usually doing, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And before he goes, Your Honour, he has one last obligation to deal with, his marking for identification of Mr. Kovacevic's report. If we let him go without finishing that which he started, we might never see him again, for all we know. To remind, Your Honour, the documents are D676, MFI, and D7677, MFI, and Mr. Hedaraly had volunteered him to deal with the issue yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I also don't want Mr. Russo to feel left out by the Gotovina Defence, so I also have an issue to raise with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They'll all keep you busy until the very end, Mr. Russo. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It relates to an issue we have with translation of Exhibit D970. I believe Mr. Kehoe advised the Court that we wanted to address the issue today with the Chamber, and we need to bring to the Chamber's attention because we have reached a impasse with CLSS, and we feel we need to bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first deal with the expert report by Mr. Kovacevic. Mr. Russo, I think you reserved your position until after we heard the testimony of Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. The Prosecution's position is that we will not object to the admission of the report but did want to make clear that this is not intended to be a lack of objection to the transparency and reliability issues which we believe are fairly significant with Mr. Kovacevic. However, in light of the Court's decision with regard to the admissibility of Professor Corn's expert report, we are taking that as guidance that these matters are simply to be addressed through the weight to be accorded. And on that basis, we are not objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D -- I think it is D7 -- no, it couldn't be. It should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 1676 and 1677, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. D1676 and D1677 are admitted into evidence. Now, Mr. Russo, your last job. Translation issues in relation to D --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could pull that, Mr. President. Or Mr. Registrar, I should say. If we could go to -- this is Mr. Rajcic's artillery order from the 2nd of August. And if we can go to page 3 in both versions, please. I'm interested in the last sentence of section 3. And the Court will recall we have had a lot of discussion about this sentence. The English has been translated as: "Shell the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac." And in the original Croatian, it says, and obviously this is the issue, but it uses the Croatian words [B/C/S spoken] and the word "udare" [phoen] here is what's of interest to us. We sent it to CLSS for a check and we now have a response back from CLSS which is that the translation should be: "Put the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire." CLSS has chosen to translate the word "udare" as "fire." But we believe that the proper translation should be "strikes." And the issue is relevant, Mr. President, because if I can turn then to the next document, which is P1272, now this is again the list of targets. And if you look in the left-hand column, along the edge, it -- in the English it's been translated as "first strike, second strike." In the original, if you look, you will see that the word "udar" is used, which is the same word that's used in the Croatian, which is to put the towns under, again the Croatian word, "udare." And so now we have the same word being used in Croatian, "udar," which is being translated by CLSS in one document as "fire," and in this document CLSS has translated it as "strike." For our purposes, what we are interested in is the consistent use or consistent translation of the same word because the Chamber may find it relevant that Mr. Rajcic, in his order, says: "Put the towns under artillery strikes," and then here we have actual specification of targets for first strike, second strike. Without going into details of why we think that would be relevant in a context of an indiscriminate shelling case. In any event, we have asked CLSS to provide us an explanation as to why the same word is being translated two different ways and they have simply stood on their position which is that they believe that the essence of the translation is accurate. But we believe that for the Chamber's purposes, it is misleading, because I think the Chamber should have the benefit of knowing that the same word is being used in both documents. At this point, we don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems that the Chamber will further consider the matter and we'll also further consider whether we need any further explanation. For example, whether if a word has several meanings that, in a certain context, for example, in one moment that it is preceded by the word first whether that changes the choice for possible translations as a contextual. I do not know whether that would be the case or would not be the case, but most important for the Chamber at this moment is to consider whether we would seek further clarification on this issue, which focuses on apparently the same word in a different contextual setting being translated by different words and not by one word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, Mr. President, we asked for a further explanation, even if it were something along those lines, and we were unable to get a response beyond that they felt it was consistent with the essence of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But also that's another way of dealing with the matter -- at least that's considering the matter is that you'd say it -- it doesn't make -- it's the same. The meaning of it is the same. We'll all have to consider whether we need further information about that or how to deal with the matter. That's the only thing I can say at this moment. It's now clearly on the record that the different words used for the translation of the word "udar" is of concern to the Gotovina Defence and that the Gotovina Defence invites the Chamber to further consider this matter. That's all that can be said about it at this moment, I take it. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour had raised, before the witness entered, the issue of The Blue Book. I don't know if we should deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, could I know, has The Blue Book been copied because it has been put on the ELMO. To the extent it came to our eyes and we can -- then, of course, it's a very cumbersome way, ask for the video and then see on the video what is on ELMO. Whereas if this is a copy available --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this is why I had gotten on my feet before the witness came, Mr. President. We have returned the physical copy to Mr. Mikulicic and thanked him for his assistance. We have scanned the physical version of the book, which, I think Mr. Carrier had indicated, we may be tendering portions or the entirety of the book. Obviously there's a translation issue still to be resolved. But the book in a scanned version, so the electronic version of what was physically in the book, is there, so a comparison can now be made between that and the electronic version that was put on the CD. We have not uploaded it. We have not tendered it yet because we are awaiting for the translation. If the Chamber is interested to have the Croatian version of the entire book that we have scanned, then, of course, we can provide that to the Chamber or deal with it in -- in whatever manner, way that the Chamber sees fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think one of the issues that came up was the use of diagrams. Now, Chamber staff, when I asked them to see if there were in the diagrams in the electronic version of The Blue Book, came up with a rather limited set of diagrams; whereas, it is my recollection, but I would have to look at the video again to see what exactly was on the ELMO, but it was one -- at least one of the more complicated -- one of the more complicated diagrams and not the relatively simple ones. So the Chamber, since the attention has been drawn to diagrams and who produced them and who may have copied or invented or scanned, or whatever, have done with that, the Chamber might be interested to have a look at the diagrams from The Blue Book. And we're not seeking, at this moment, to have the whole of The Blue Book to be translated but, rather, to look at the diagrams. So for transparency purposes, I wished to raise the matter in court and not to ask in any other way. But the Chamber would have -- would like to have a look at the diagrams as they appear The Blue Book, and gives an opportunities to the parties to comment, if the parties would consider that this is not what the Chamber should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would the Chamber want the translations of the diagrams as well? I assume that would not take -- before handing it over or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. It could well be that if the same diagrams do appear elsewhere that -- and if the text is the same, then, of course, we wouldn't ask for any additional translation. But we'd first just like to have a look at them and then perhaps come back to the issue at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, we will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you please be so kind to -- whatever you send to us, to send a copy to the other parties, so that the parties are -- that the Defence teams are fully aware of what has been brought to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course, and that is our common practice as well. On the related issue, Mr. Feldi was asked about two documents that he was going to provide the Chamber. One of them was the contract, and the other was the order of appointment for the preparation of The Blue Book. We have received one of these two documents via the Registry, and I just want to put that on the record that it's in Croatian. I think it looks like a contract, but the second one is still pending, and I just wanted to put that on the record to see if we can make sure that we also received the second document that is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We haven't received that, so whoever is sending documents to the Prosecution, if they could remember that the other parties have an interest as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From my previous remark it may be clear already that the Chamber considers this also important that there is full transparency on any material. May I take it, Mr. Hedaraly, that whatever you have received, that you will disclose a copy to the Defence teams, and then if you receive any further documents, that you would do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kay, you have produced two Internet pages, in relation to the last witness. Well, if -- do you have any -- did you want to tender them? I think the best thing to do is to -- to print them out from the Internet and then to file them, or to file the precise page identification. The problem is that, of course, a page can be changed over time. So, therefore, I think a quick printout of -- I think it was one from the HINA web site and the other one from the international Helsinki Committee, that would create the transparency we need, that everyone, including possibly the Appeals Chamber, would know what we looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Firstly, they were both read into the record, so that has been dealt with, and they were seen on the screen here. So the matters have been recorded. We will upload them into e-court and get numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's another way of dealing with the matter. I do remember that you read the second one. It's just a lack of recollection whether you fully read the first one. And what I do remember is that we started looking at a certain page, whereas, I think, it was me, myself, who later said, This is the annual report of 1997 coming from this and this and this, so that we have the context. But if we have the Internet page uploaded then we have all the information we would need. Then once it has been uploaded, I take it that you -- you will take the initiative to tender it. And may I already establish that there is no objection. Mr. Russo, perhaps one of your last official -- no. Mr. Hedaraly will whisper into your ear whether you should object or not and then that would be your last ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I hate to go out with a whimper, Your Honour, but we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then once uploaded, it's ready to be admitted into evidence. No other matters at this moment. Then we will adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 30th of September, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of September, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.40 p.m.,
